claim: Early-life experiences may promote stereotyped behavioral alterations that are dynamic across development time.
source: Early-life experiences may promote stereotyped behavioral alterations that are dynamic across development time, but also behavioral responses that are variable among individuals, even when initially exposed to the same stimulus.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a general premise of the study.

claim: Early-life experiences may promote behavioral responses that are variable among individuals, even when initially exposed to the same stimulus.
source: Early-life experiences may promote stereotyped behavioral alterations that are dynamic across development time, but also behavioral responses that are variable among individuals, even when initially exposed to the same stimulus.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a general premise of the study.

claim: Behavioral effects of early-life starvation are exposed during early and late developmental stages.
source: Here, by utilizing longitudinal monitoring of Caenorhabditis elegans individuals throughout development we show that behavioral effects of early-life starvation are exposed during early and late developmental stages and buffered during intermediate stages of development.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1.

claim: Behavioral effects of early-life starvation are buffered during intermediate stages of development.
source: Here, by utilizing longitudinal monitoring of Caenorhabditis elegans individuals throughout development we show that behavioral effects of early-life starvation are exposed during early and late developmental stages and buffered during intermediate stages of development.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1.

claim: Both dopamine and serotonin shape the discontinuous behavioral responses by opposite and temporally segregated functions across development time.
source: We further found that both dopamine and serotonin shape the discontinuous behavioral responses by opposite and temporally segregated functions across development time.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data shown in Figures 3-5.

claim: Dopamine buffers behavioral responses during intermediate developmental stages.
source: While dopamine buffers behavioral responses during intermediate developmental stages, serotonin promotes behavioral sensitivity to stress during early and late stages.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data shown in Figures 3-4.

claim: Serotonin promotes behavioral sensitivity to stress during early and late stages.
source: While dopamine buffers behavioral responses during intermediate developmental stages, serotonin promotes behavioral sensitivity to stress during early and late stages.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5.

claim: Unsupervised analysis of individual biases across development uncovered multiple individuality dimensions that coexist within stressed and unstressed populations.
source: Interestingly, unsupervised analysis of individual biases across development uncovered multiple individuality dimensions that coexist within stressed and unstressed populations and further identified experience-dependent effects on variation within specific individuality dimensions.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2.

claim: Experience-dependent effects on variation within specific individuality dimensions were identified.
source: Interestingly, unsupervised analysis of individual biases across development uncovered multiple individuality dimensions that coexist within stressed and unstressed populations and further identified experience-dependent effects on variation within specific individuality dimensions.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6.

claim: Flies show differences in foraging behavior that depend on their larval stage.
source: For instance, flies show differences in foraging behavior that depend on their larval stage (Sokolowski et al., 1984), fish internally modify their startle response across life (Kimmel et al., 1974) and stomatogastric motor patterns are regulated across development (Rehm et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Sokolowski et al., 1984.

claim: Fish internally modify their startle response across life.
source: For instance, flies show differences in foraging behavior that depend on their larval stage (Sokolowski et al., 1984), fish internally modify their startle response across life (Kimmel et al., 1974) and stomatogastric motor patterns are regulated across development (Rehm et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Kimmel et al., 1974.

claim: Stomatogastric motor patterns are regulated across development.
source: For instance, flies show differences in foraging behavior that depend on their larval stage (Sokolowski et al., 1984), fish internally modify their startle response across life (Kimmel et al., 1974) and stomatogastric motor patterns are regulated across development (Rehm et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Rehm et al., 2008.

claim: Fear-extinction learning is inhibited during adolescence compared to other life stages in humans and mice.
source: In addition, fear-extinction learning is inhibited during adolescence compared to other life stages in humans and mice (Pattwell et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Pattwell et al., 2012.

claim: Experiences during early developmental windows were shown to generate long-lasting effects.
source: In particular, animals may be transiently exposed to environmental perturbations at different stages of life, but experiences during early developmental windows, which are usually referred to as critical or sensitive periods, were shown to generate long-lasting effects (Lorenz, 1935; Korosi et al., 2012; Jin et al., 2016; Nevitt et al., 1994; Remy and Hobert, 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Lorenz, 1935; Korosi et al., 2012; Jin et al., 2016; Nevitt et al., 1994; Remy and Hobert, 2005.

claim: Stable imprinting of early memories has the potential to increase survival and reproduction during later life stages of the organism.
source: This stable imprinting of early memories has the potential to increase survival and reproduction during later life stages of the organism (Immelmann, 1975).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Immelmann, 1975.

claim: Consistent behavioral individuality within isogenic populations that were raised in the same environment has been previously described in various species.
source: Consistent behavioral individuality within isogenic populations that were raised in the same environment has been previously described in various species, including in the pea aphid (Schuett et al., 2011), Drosophila melanogaster (Buchanan et al., 2015; Kain et al., 2012; Linneweber et al., 2020), clonal fish (Bierbach et al., 2017), and mice (Freund et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Schuett et al., 2011; Buchanan et al., 2015; Kain et al., 2012; Linneweber et al., 2020; Bierbach et al., 2017; Freund et al., 2013.

claim: C. elegans is an ideal system to study how early-life experiences shape long-term behavior and inter-individual variation across developmental timescales due to their short development time of 2.5 days.
source: The nematode Caenorhabditis elegans is an ideal system to study how early-life experiences shape long-term behavior and inter-individual variation across developmental timescales due to their short development time of 2.5 days and the homogeneous populations generated by the self-fertilizing reproduction mode of the hermaphrodite.
evidence: This is stated as a rationale for using C. elegans and is based on established knowledge about the organism.

claim: C. elegans is an ideal system to study how early-life experiences shape long-term behavior and inter-individual variation across developmental timescales due to the homogeneous populations generated by the self-fertilizing reproduction mode of the hermaphrodite.
source: The nematode Caenorhabditis elegans is an ideal system to study how early-life experiences shape long-term behavior and inter-individual variation across developmental timescales due to their short development time of 2.5 days and the homogeneous populations generated by the self-fertilizing reproduction mode of the hermaphrodite.
evidence: This is stated as a rationale for using C. elegans and is based on established knowledge about the organism.

claim: Under normal growth conditions, C. elegans shows both stereotypic patterns of long-term behavior and consistent individual biases within the isogenic population.
source: It was previously shown that under normal growth conditions, C. elegans shows both stereotypic patterns of long-term behavior and consistent individual biases within the isogenic population (Stern et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Stern et al., 2017.

claim: First larval stage (L1) animals that hatch into an environment that completely lacks a food source do not grow and their development is arrested.
source: First larval stage (L1) animals that hatch into an environment that completely lacks a food source do not grow and their development is arrested (Greenwald and Horvitz, 1982; Johnson et al., 1984; Baugh, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Greenwald and Horvitz, 1982; Johnson et al., 1984; Baugh, 2013.

claim: Following L1 arrest, when animals encounter food, they resume their normal developmental trajectory to reach adulthood.
source: Following L1 arrest, when animals encounter food, they resume their normal developmental trajectory to reach adulthood.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about C. elegans development.

claim: Animals exposed to early starvation required more time to complete their development.
source: Animals exposed to early starvation required more time to complete their development (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Whilst growing in a food environment, C. elegans shifts between two behavioral states called roaming and dwelling that last seconds to minutes.
source: Whilst growing in a food environment, C. elegans shifts between two behavioral states called roaming and dwelling that last seconds to minutes (Ben Arous et al., 2009; Flavell et al., 2013; Fujiwara et al., 2002; Stern et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Ben Arous et al., 2009; Flavell et al., 2013; Fujiwara et al., 2002; Stern et al., 2017.

claim: During a roaming episode animals explore a large area by high-speed forward movements.
source: During a roaming episode animals explore a large area by high-speed forward movements, while in the dwelling episode they show dramatically less exploration due to low-speed movements coupled with frequent reorientations (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge and illustrated in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claim: In the dwelling episode animals show dramatically less exploration due to low-speed movements coupled with frequent reorientations.
source: During a roaming episode animals explore a large area by high-speed forward movements, while in the dwelling episode they show dramatically less exploration due to low-speed movements coupled with frequent reorientations (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge and illustrated in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Unstressed individuals hatching in a food environment show dynamic behavioral structures of roaming activity across development.
source: Unstressed individuals hatching in a food environment show dynamic behavioral structures of roaming activity across development, as was previously shown (Stern et al., 2017; Figure 1B–D).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Stern et al., 2017 and data shown in Figure 1B-D.

claim: A short early-starvation period of 1 day strongly decreased average roaming activity levels during the L1 and adult stages compared to unstressed individuals.
source: We found that a transient exposure to early-life starvation generates alterations in long-term behavioral patterns throughout development that were distinct and discontinuous across and within developmental stages. A short early-starvation period of 1 day strongly decreased average roaming activity levels during the L1 and adult stages compared to unstressed individuals (Figure 1C, E; Figure 1—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1C, E and Figure 1—figure supplement 1D.

claim: While 1 day of early starvation modified within-stage temporal behavioral structures by shifting roaming activity peaks to later time windows during the L2 and L3 stages, average roaming activity was not decreased during these stages.
source: In contrast, while 1 day of early starvation modified within-stage temporal behavioral structures by shifting roaming activity peaks to later time windows during the L2 and L3 stages (Figure 1C; Figure 1—figure supplement 1E), average roaming activity was not decreased during these stages (Figure 1E).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1C, E and Figure 1—figure supplement 1E.

claim: Average roaming activity level was maintained during the L4 stage, following 1-day starvation.
source: Similarly, we found that average roaming activity level was also maintained during the L4 stage, following 1-day starvation (Figure 1C, E; Figure 1—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1C, E and Figure 1—figure supplement 1D.

claim: Animals exposed to longer starvation periods of 3 and 4 days showed strong roaming decrease during L1 and adulthood, but exhibited only minor effects on average roaming activity within the intermediate L2, L3, and L4 larval stages.
source: Interestingly, animals exposed to longer starvation periods of 3 and 4 days further showed strong roaming decrease during L1 and adulthood, but exhibited only minor effects on average roaming activity within the intermediate L2, L3, and L4 larval stages (Figure 1D, E; Figure 1—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1D, E and Figure 1—figure supplement 1D.

claim: The average size of animals that experienced early starvation was slightly decreased (~10%).
source: Furthermore, while the average size of animals that experienced early starvation was slightly decreased (~10%), a comparison of starved and unstarved individuals within the same size range (size-matched) showed similar stage-specific effects on roaming activity during L1 and adulthood following early starvation (Figure 1—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1F.

claim: A comparison of starved and unstarved individuals within the same size range (size-matched) showed similar stage-specific effects on roaming activity during L1 and adulthood following early starvation.
source: Furthermore, while the average size of animals that experienced early starvation was slightly decreased (~10%), a comparison of starved and unstarved individuals within the same size range (size-matched) showed similar stage-specific effects on roaming activity during L1 and adulthood following early starvation (Figure 1—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1F.

claim: Instantaneous speed during roaming episodes in individuals exposed to early starvation was affected more strongly at the L1 and adult stages, compared to the intermediate stages.
source: Similar to the stage-specific effects of early starvation on the fraction of time spent roaming, instantaneous speed during roaming episodes in individuals exposed to early starvation was affected more strongly at the L1 and adult stages, compared to the intermediate stages (Figure 1—figure supplement 1G).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1G.

claim: Following early starvation, different individuals show substantial variation in long-term behavioral responses.
source: Following early starvation, different individuals show substantial variation in long-term behavioral responses.
evidence: This is stated as an observation from the data.

claim: During L1 and adulthood, a fraction of wild-type individuals that were exposed to early stress show 8- to 10-fold decrease in roaming activity relative to the average roaming level of the unstressed population, while other stressed individuals show roaming activity which is indistinguishable from unstressed animals.
source: For instance, during L1 and adulthood, a fraction of wild-type individuals that were exposed to early stress show 8- to 10-fold decrease in roaming activity relative to the average roaming level of the unstressed population, while other stressed individuals show roaming activity which is indistinguishable from unstressed animals (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1D.

claim: Behavioral individuality is usually defined as a consistent tendency of an individual to show the same behavioral bias relative to the population across long time-periods.
source: Behavioral individuality is usually defined as a consistent tendency of an individual to show the same behavioral bias relative to the population across long time-periods (Bierbach et al., 2017; Buchanan et al., 2015; Kain et al., 2012; Stern et al., 2017; Schuett et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Bierbach et al., 2017; Buchanan et al., 2015; Kain et al., 2012; Stern et al., 2017; Schuett et al., 2011.

claim: PC1, which explained the majority of temporal variation in individual biases over time had eigenvector components of the same sign, indicating an individuality dimension of animals that consistently roam more or less than the population homogeneously across all developmental stages.
source: PC1, which explained the majority of temporal variation in individual biases over time had eigenvector components of the same sign, indicating an individuality dimension of animals that consistently roam more or less than the population homogeneously across all developmental stages (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: The individuality dimension identified by PC1 unbiasedly recaptured a known mode of consistent individuality that was previously identified using a pre-defined index of long-term behavioral consistency across development.
source: The individuality dimension identified by PC1 unbiasedly recaptured a known mode of consistent individuality that was previously identified using a pre-defined index of long-term behavioral consistency across development (Stern et al., 2017; Figure 2—figure supplement 1C, D).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Stern et al., 2017 and data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1C, D.

claim: There is a high correlation between the pre-defined consistency index and scores of PC1 across individuals (R = 0.9).
source: This was further verified by the high correlation between the pre-defined consistency index and scores of PC1 across individuals (R = 0.9) (Figure 2—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1E.

claim: PC2, which had opposite signs of eigenvector components before and after mid-development captured an individuality dimension that includes individuals that switch their behavioral bias once, during the L3 stage, from roaming more to roaming less than the population and vice versa.
source: PC2, which had opposite signs of eigenvector components before and after mid-development captured an individuality dimension that includes individuals that switch their behavioral bias once, during the L3 stage, from roaming more to roaming less than the population and vice versa (Figure 2E).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: PC3, which had signs of eigenvector components that switch twice during development (at the end of L1 and L4), identified individuals that show the same behavioral bias during L1 and adulthood, which is opposite to their behavioral bias during intermediate stages.
source: In addition, PC3, which had signs of eigenvector components that switch twice during development (at the end of L1 and L4), identified individuals that show the same behavioral bias during L1 and adulthood, which is opposite to their behavioral bias during intermediate stages (Figure 2F).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2F.

claim: PC individual scores in alternative PC dimensions did not correlate with the pre-defined consistency index (R = 0.003–0.09).
source: PC individual scores in these alternative PC dimensions did not correlate with the pre-defined consistency index (R = 0.003–0.09) (Figure 2—figure supplement 1E), further indicating that they indeed represent uncharacterized modes of temporal individuality.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1E.

claim: Wild-type populations with different early-life experiences show extreme inter-individual variation in multiple PC dimensions, compared to a randomly shuffled rank dataset.
source: We found that wild-type populations with different early-life experiences show extreme inter-individual variation in multiple PC dimensions, compared to a randomly shuffled rank dataset within the same PCA space or within a PCA space generated from the shuffled rank dataset (Figure 2G–J; Figure 2—figure supplement 1G, H), indicating the coexistence of these alternative individuality dimensions.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2G-J and Figure 2—figure supplement 1G, H.

claim: Neuromodulatory pathways are known to establish internal behavioral states and modify them based on the environmental context.
source: Neuromodulatory pathways are known to establish internal behavioral states and modify them based on the environmental context (Harris-Warrick and Marder, 1991; Bargmann, 2012; Marder, 2012; Kennedy et al., 2014; Taghert and Nitabach, 2012; Nusbaum and Blitz, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Harris-Warrick and Marder, 1991; Bargmann, 2012; Marder, 2012; Kennedy et al., 2014; Taghert and Nitabach, 2012; Nusbaum and Blitz, 2012.

claim: The bioamine dopamine was implicated in controlling a wide array of behavioral outputs at various timescales, ranging from minutes and hours, to long-term behavioral patterns that are regulated across life stages.
source: In particular, the bioamine dopamine was implicated in controlling a wide array of behavioral outputs at various timescales, ranging from minutes and hours, to long-term behavioral patterns that are regulated across life stages (Marella et al., 2012; Omura et al., 2012; Sawin et al., 2000; Cermak et al., 2020; Stern et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Marella et al., 2012; Omura et al., 2012; Sawin et al., 2000; Cermak et al., 2020; Stern et al., 2017.

claim: In C. elegans, dopamine is produced in a specific set of neuronal sites.
source: In C. elegans, dopamine is produced in a specific set of neuronal sites and its effects are known to be mediated by dopamine receptors that are localized to responding neurons (Sulston et al., 1975; Lints and Emmons, 1999; Chase et al., 2004; Tsalik et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Sulston et al., 1975; Lints and Emmons, 1999; Chase et al., 2004; Tsalik et al., 2003.

claim: Dopamine effects are known to be mediated by dopamine receptors that are localized to responding neurons.
source: In C. elegans, dopamine is produced in a specific set of neuronal sites and its effects are known to be mediated by dopamine receptors that are localized to responding neurons (Sulston et al., 1975; Lints and Emmons, 1999; Chase et al., 2004; Tsalik et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Sulston et al., 1975; Lints and Emmons, 1999; Chase et al., 2004; Tsalik et al., 2003.

claim: When continuously grown in a food environment, cat-2 individuals show a long-term roaming activity pattern that is similar to the wild-type population.
source: When continuously grown in a food environment, cat-2 individuals show a long-term roaming activity pattern that is similar to the wild-type population (Stern et al., 2017; Figure 1; Figure 3).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Stern et al., 2017 and data shown in Figure 1 and Figure 3.

claim: In contrast to stressed wild-type individuals that show buffering of behavioral responses during the L2, L3, and L4 intermediate stages, cat-2 individuals that were exposed to early starvation show reduction in average roaming activity across all developmental stages, including during the intermediate stages.
source: However, we found that in contrast to stressed wild-type individuals that show buffering of behavioral responses during the L2, L3, and L4 intermediate stages, cat-2 individuals that were exposed to early starvation show reduction in average roaming activity across all developmental stages, including during the intermediate stages (Figure 3B, C).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 3B, C.

claim: The behavioral effects of early starvation during mid-development in cat-2 individuals were not only restricted to animals that were exposed to long starvation periods, as 1 day of early starvation was sufficient to induce a strong reduction in roaming activity during the L2–L4 intermediate stages.
source: The behavioral effects of early starvation during mid-development in cat-2 individuals were not only restricted to animals that were exposed to long starvation periods, as 1 day of early starvation was sufficient to induce a strong reduction in roaming activity during the L2–L4 intermediate stages (Figure 3D; Figure 3—figure supplement 1B–D).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 3D and Figure 3—figure supplement 1B-D.

claim: During the L2 intermediate stage the effects on roaming activity patterns were more pronounced during earlier time windows of the stage, suggesting a potential within-stage regulation of behavioral response by dopamine.
source: Interestingly, during the L2 intermediate stage the effects on roaming activity patterns were more pronounced during earlier time windows of the stage, suggesting a potential within-stage regulation of behavioral response by dopamine (Figure 3B, C; Figure 3—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 3B, C and Figure 3—figure supplement 1C, and involves inference from the observed pattern.

claim: Behavioral effects during L1 and adulthood following early stress were similar in cat-2 and wild-type.
source: However, behavioral effects during L1 and adulthood following early stress were similar in cat-2 and wild-type (Figure 3B–D), implying that dopamine function is mainly required during intermediate developmental stages to buffer alterations in roaming activity in response to a transient early stress.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 3B-D.

claim: Dopamine function is mainly required during intermediate developmental stages to buffer alterations in roaming activity in response to a transient early stress.
source: However, behavioral effects during L1 and adulthood following early stress were similar in cat-2 and wild-type (Figure 3B–D), implying that dopamine function is mainly required during intermediate developmental stages to buffer alterations in roaming activity in response to a transient early stress.
evidence: This is inferred from the comparison of cat-2 and wild-type data shown in Figure 3B-D.

claim: During L2 to adulthood, cat-2 animals have higher instantaneous speed during roaming episodes.
source: It was previously shown that during L2 to adulthood, cat-2 animals have higher instantaneous speed during roaming episodes (Stern et al., 2017; Sawin et al., 2000; Figure 3—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Stern et al., 2017; Sawin et al., 2000 and data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1E.

claim: Unlike stressed wild-type individuals in which roaming speed was decreased mainly during L1 and adulthood, cat-2 mutants show lower speed also across the L2 and L3 stages following stress.
source: We found that unlike stressed wild-type individuals in which roaming speed was decreased mainly during L1 and adulthood (Figure 1—figure supplement 1G), cat-2 mutants show lower speed also across the L2 and L3 stages following stress (Figure 3—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1G and Figure 3—figure supplement 1F.

claim: Supplementing dopamine was sufficient to increase only the roaming activity following stress in cat-2 individuals exposed to 1 and 3 days of starvation, during the L2, L3, and L4 stages.
source: We found that supplementing dopamine was sufficient to increase only the roaming activity following stress in cat-2 individuals exposed to 1 and 3 days of starvation, during the L2, L3, and L4 stages (Figure 4A–C; Figure 4—figure supplement 1B, C, F, G).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 4A-C and Figure 4—figure supplement 1B, C, F, G.

claim: Following 1 day of starvation exogenous dopamine did not restore roaming activity during L1 and adulthood.
source: In contrast, following 1 day of starvation exogenous dopamine did not restore roaming activity during L1 and adulthood (Figure 4A, C; Figure 4—figure supplement 1A, B) and following 3 days of starvation it only slightly increased roaming in the L1 stage and did not affect roaming activity during adulthood (Figure 4B, C; Figure 4—figure supplement 1A, C).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 4A, C and Figure 4—figure supplement 1A, B.

claim: Following 3 days of starvation exogenous dopamine only slightly increased roaming in the L1 stage and did not affect roaming activity during adulthood.
source: In contrast, following 1 day of starvation exogenous dopamine did not restore roaming activity during L1 and adulthood (Figure 4A, C; Figure 4—figure supplement 1A, B) and following 3 days of starvation it only slightly increased roaming in the L1 stage and did not affect roaming activity during adulthood (Figure 4B, C; Figure 4—figure supplement 1A, C).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 4B, C and Figure 4—figure supplement 1A, C.

claim: The C. elegans dopamine receptor DOP-1 is a D1-like receptor which signal through Gαs/olf to activate adenylyl cyclase.
source: The C. elegans dopamine receptor DOP-1 is a D1-like receptor which signal through Gαs/olf to activate adenylyl cyclase and DOP-2 and DOP-3 receptors are D2-like receptors which signal via Gαi to suppress adenylyl cyclase (Chase et al., 2004; Sanyal et al., 2004; Sugiura et al., 2005; Suo et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Chase et al., 2004; Sanyal et al., 2004; Sugiura et al., 2005; Suo et al., 2003.

claim: DOP-2 and DOP-3 receptors are D2-like receptors which signal via Gαi to suppress adenylyl cyclase.
source: The C. elegans dopamine receptor DOP-1 is a D1-like receptor which signal through Gαs/olf to activate adenylyl cyclase and DOP-2 and DOP-3 receptors are D2-like receptors which signal via Gαi to suppress adenylyl cyclase (Chase et al., 2004; Sanyal et al., 2004; Sugiura et al., 2005; Suo et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Chase et al., 2004; Sanyal et al., 2004; Sugiura et al., 2005; Suo et al., 2003.

claim: Each dopamine receptor has a different temporal effect on behavioral responses within the intermediate L2–L4 stages.
source: To study the independent function of dopamine receptors we analyzed the long-term behavioral effects of early starvation in animals mutant for each of the single dopamine receptors. These analyses showed that each receptor has a different temporal effect on behavioral responses within the intermediate L2–L4 stages (Figure 4D–I; Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 4D-I and Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: Following 3 days of early starvation, dop-2 animals showed strong roaming decrease during the L2 and L4 stages, but not during the L3 stage, compared to wild-type.
source: In particular, following 3 days of early starvation, dop-2 animals showed strong roaming decrease during the L2 and L4 stages, but not during the L3 stage, compared to wild-type (Figure 4D, G; Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 4D, G and Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: Similar to cat-2 mutants, roaming was mainly decreased in dop-2 individuals during early time windows within the L2 stage.
source: Interestingly, similar to cat-2 mutants, roaming was mainly decreased in dop-2 individuals during early time windows within the L2 stage.
evidence: This is stated as an observation from the data.

claim: dop-1 individuals showed a roaming decrease during the L2 stage and opposite effects during L3 and L4.
source: In addition, dop-1 individuals showed a roaming decrease during the L2 stage and opposite effects during L3 and L4 (Figure 4E, H; Figure 4—figure supplement 2) and dop-3 animals showed weaker overall roaming response during the L2 stage (Figure 4F, I; Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 4E, H and Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: dop-3 animals showed weaker overall roaming response during the L2 stage.
source: In addition, dop-1 individuals showed a roaming decrease during the L2 stage and opposite effects during L3 and L4 (Figure 4E, H; Figure 4—figure supplement 2) and dop-3 animals showed weaker overall roaming response during the L2 stage (Figure 4F, I; Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 4F, I and Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: DOP-2 and DOP-3 were shown to function cooperatively.
source: Previously, DOP-2 and DOP-3 were shown to function cooperatively (Cermak et al., 2020; Suo et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Cermak et al., 2020; Suo et al., 2009.

claim: Following early starvation, dop-2;dop-3 double mutants showed a decreased roaming activity across all intermediate stages.
source: We found that following early starvation, dop-2;dop-3 double mutants showed a decreased roaming activity across all intermediate stages (Figure 4J, K; Figure 4—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 4J, K and Figure 4—figure supplement 3.

claim: A deficiency in both DOP-2 and DOP-3 receptors is sufficient to recapitulate the behavioral effects in dopamine-deficient individuals during mid-development.
source: These results imply that a deficiency in both DOP-2 and DOP-3 receptors is sufficient to recapitulate the behavioral effects in dopamine-deficient individuals during mid-development and suggest that buffering of long-term behavioral responses by dopamine is temporally regulated by the modular function of specific dopamine receptors.
evidence: This is inferred from the comparison of dop-2;dop-3 double mutants and cat-2 mutants.

claim: Buffering of long-term behavioral responses by dopamine is temporally regulated by the modular function of specific dopamine receptors.
source: These results imply that a deficiency in both DOP-2 and DOP-3 receptors is sufficient to recapitulate the behavioral effects in dopamine-deficient individuals during mid-development and suggest that buffering of long-term behavioral responses by dopamine is temporally regulated by the modular function of specific dopamine receptors.
evidence: This is inferred from the analysis of single and double dopamine receptor mutants.

claim: Under normal growth conditions, serotonin-deficient tph-1 individuals roam more than wild-type across all developmental stages.
source: Under normal growth conditions, serotonin-deficient tph-1 individuals roam more than wild-type across all developmental stages (Flavell et al., 2013; Stern et al., 2017; Figure 5—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Flavell et al., 2013; Stern et al., 2017 and data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1B.

claim: tph-1 individuals that were exposed to 1 day of early starvation maintained their roaming activity during L1 and adulthood, compared to the strong roaming decrease generated in the wild-type population during these early and late stages.
source: We found that contrary to the effects of dopamine on the buffering of behavioral responses during intermediate stages, tph-1 individuals that were exposed to 1 day of early starvation maintained their roaming activity during L1 and adulthood (Figure 5B, D; Figure 5—figure supplement 1C), compared to the strong roaming decrease generated in the wild-type population during these early and late stages.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 5B, D and Figure 5—figure supplement 1C.

claim: No significant difference in roaming response was shown during the L2–L4 intermediate developmental stages in the tph-1 population following 1 day of early starvation, compared to wild-type.
source: In addition, no significant difference in roaming response was shown during the L2–L4 intermediate developmental stages in the tph-1 population following 1 day of early starvation (Figure 5B, D; Figure 5—figure supplement 1C), compared to wild-type.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 5B, D and Figure 5—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Long starvation periods led to a reduction in roaming activity in the L1 stage of tph-1 animals.
source: We found that long starvation periods led to a reduction in roaming activity in the L1 stage of tph-1 animals. However, during the adult stage, tph-1 individuals were still less responsive to early stress, compared to the strong decrease in roaming in the wild-type (Figure 5C, D; Figure 5—figure supplement 1C, D).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 5C, D and Figure 5—figure supplement 1C, D.

claim: During the adult stage, tph-1 individuals were still less responsive to early stress, compared to the strong decrease in roaming in the wild-type.
source: We found that long starvation periods led to a reduction in roaming activity in the L1 stage of tph-1 animals. However, during the adult stage, tph-1 individuals were still less responsive to early stress, compared to the strong decrease in roaming in the wild-type (Figure 5C, D; Figure 5—figure supplement 1C, D).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 5C, D and Figure 5—figure supplement 1C, D.

claim: Behavioral responses to early stress were similar in tph-1 and wild-type individuals during the intermediate L2–L4 stages, indicating that serotonin effects are specific to shaping behavioral responses during L1 and adulthood.
source: In addition, behavioral responses to early stress were similar in tph-1 and wild-type individuals during the intermediate L2–L4 stages, indicating that serotonin effects are specific to shaping behavioral responses during L1 and adulthood.
evidence: This is inferred from the comparison of tph-1 and wild-type data.

claim: Dopamine and serotonin functions are opposite and segregated across developmental stages in regulating long-term roaming behavior following stress.
source: These results show that dopamine and serotonin functions are opposite and segregated across developmental stages in regulating long-term roaming behavior following stress.
evidence: This is inferred from the combined analysis of dopamine and serotonin mutants.

claim: Functional segregation among dopamine and serotonin regulation is behavior specific, as the long-term effects of early stress on roaming speed were similar in tph-1 and cat-2 individuals.
source: Interestingly, functional segregation among dopamine and serotonin regulation is behavior specific, as the long-term effects of early stress on roaming speed were similar in tph-1 and cat-2 individuals (Figure 5—figure supplement 1E; Figure 3—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1E and Figure 3—figure supplement 1F.

claim: Both the wild-type and dopamine-deficient cat-2 populations showed an increase in inter-individual variation in PC scores within the PC3 individuality dimension following starvation, compared to the unstressed population.
source: In particular, both the wild-type and dopamine-deficient cat-2 populations showed an increase in inter-individual variation in PC scores within the PC3 individuality dimension (double bias switching across development) following starvation, compared to the unstressed population (Figure 6B, D, F).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 6B, D, F.

claim: Inter-individual variation in scores within the PC3 dimension was not significantly altered in serotonin-deficient tph-1 individuals following the same stressful experiences.
source: In contrast, inter-individual variation in scores within the PC3 dimension was not significantly altered in serotonin-deficient tph-1 individuals following the same stressful experiences (Figure 6B, E).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 6B, E.

claim: Inter-individual variation in scores within the PC6 individuality dimension was strongly increased following all stressful conditions in the wild-type population, but was decreased after 3 days of early starvation in the tph-1 population.
source: Furthermore, we found that inter-individual variation in scores within the PC6 individuality dimension which captured multiple bias switching of individuals within developmental stages (L2-Adulthood) was strongly increased following all stressful conditions in the wild-type population, but was decreased after 3 days of early starvation in the tph-1 population (Figure 6C–E).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 6C-E.

claim: cat-2 individuals did not show altered PC6 inter-individual variation after early-life stress.
source: While inter-individual variation in PC6 was affected in opposite directions in the wild-type and tph-1 populations following stress, cat-2 individuals did not show altered PC6 inter-individual variation after early-life stress (Figure 6C, F).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 6C, F.

claim: Unstarved tph-1 individuals show low levels of behavioral consistency across development compared to the wild-type population, as quantified by the pre-defined consistency index.
source: In addition, it was previously shown that unstarved tph-1 individuals show low levels of behavioral consistency across development compared to the wild-type population, as quantified by the pre-defined consistency index (Stern et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Stern et al., 2017.

claim: Unstarved tph-1 individuals show lower levels of inter-individual variation in PC scores within the PC1 dimension, compared to the wild-type population.
source: Similarly, we found that unstarved tph-1 individuals show lower levels of inter-individual variation in PC scores within the PC1 dimension, which represents individuals with homogenous consistent bias across development, compared to the wild-type population (Figure 6—figure supplement 1D; Figure 6E).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1D and Figure 6E.

claim: 3- and 4-day starved tph-1 individuals showed an increase in inter-individual variation in scores within the PC1 individuality dimension, compared to unstressed individuals, while in the wild-type and cat-2 populations there was no significant change following starvation.
source: Interestingly, we found that 3- and 4-day starved tph-1 individuals showed an increase in inter-individual variation in scores within the PC1 individuality dimension, compared to unstressed individuals, while in the wild-type and cat-2 populations there was no significant change following starvation (Figure 6A, D–F).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 6A, D-F.

claim: Inter-individual variation in scores was not significantly altered following early stress within the PC2, PC4, and PC5 individuality dimensions in all wild-type and neuromodulatory mutant populations.
source: Early starvation affected only a fraction of the identified individuality dimensions as inter-individual variation in scores was not significantly altered following early stress within the PC2, PC4, and PC5 individuality dimensions in all wild-type and neuromodulatory mutant populations (Figure 6—figure supplement 1F–H).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1F-H.

claim: Inter-individual variation in a spectrum of individuality dimensions may be dynamically structured by the early experience of the population and be further modified by its neuromodulatory state.
source: Overall, these results imply that inter-individual variation in a spectrum of individuality dimensions may be dynamically structured by the early experience of the population and be further modified by its neuromodulatory state.
evidence: This is inferred from the combined analysis of individuality dimensions across different genotypes and starvation conditions.

claim: Temporal differences in long-term behavioral responses to early stress are reflected by strong behavioral modifications during early and late developmental stages and the buffering of behavioral effects during intermediate stages of development.
source: Temporal differences in long-term behavioral responses to early stress are reflected by strong behavioral modifications during early and late developmental stages and the buffering of behavioral effects during intermediate stages of development.
evidence: This is a summary statement of the main findings.

claim: Dopamine maintains the buffering of behavioral responses during mid-development.
source: We further found that dopamine maintains the buffering of behavioral responses during mid-development and serotonin promotes behavioral sensitivity to early starvation during early and late stages of development.
evidence: This is a summary statement of the main findings.

claim: Serotonin promotes behavioral sensitivity to early starvation during early and late stages of development.
source: We further found that dopamine maintains the buffering of behavioral responses during mid-development and serotonin promotes behavioral sensitivity to early starvation during early and late stages of development.
evidence: This is a summary statement of the main findings.

claim: In C. elegans, dopamine is produced in four pairs of neurons: CEPV, CEPD, ADE, and PDE.
source: In C. elegans, dopamine is produced in four pairs of neurons: CEPV, CEPD, ADE, and PDE (Sulston et al., 1975; Lints and Emmons, 1999) and was shown to be required for controlling locomotory patterns (Omura et al., 2012) and coupling of behavioral programs (Cermak et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Sulston et al., 1975; Lints and Emmons, 1999.

claim: Dopamine was shown to be required for controlling locomotory patterns.
source: In C. elegans, dopamine is produced in four pairs of neurons: CEPV, CEPD, ADE, and PDE (Sulston et al., 1975; Lints and Emmons, 1999) and was shown to be required for controlling locomotory patterns (Omura et al., 2012) and coupling of behavioral programs (Cermak et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Omura et al., 2012.

claim: Dopamine was shown to be required for coupling of behavioral programs.
source: In C. elegans, dopamine is produced in four pairs of neurons: CEPV, CEPD, ADE, and PDE (Sulston et al., 1975; Lints and Emmons, 1999) and was shown to be required for controlling locomotory patterns (Omura et al., 2012) and coupling of behavioral programs (Cermak et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Cermak et al., 2020.

claim: Dopamine was shown to decrease the instantaneous speed of worms grown on food, compared to non-food environment.
source: In particular, dopamine was shown to decrease the instantaneous speed of worms grown on food, compared to non-food environment (Sawin et al., 2000).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Sawin et al., 2000.

claim: Dopamine function is variable under different environmental contexts and at different timescales.
source: These diverse behavioral effects on different locomotory parameters suggest that dopamine function is variable under different environmental contexts and at different timescales.
evidence: This is inferred from the comparison of dopamine effects under different conditions.

claim: The expression patterns of the three dopamine receptors within the C. elegans nervous system are partially overlapping.
source: Interestingly, the expression patterns of the three dopamine receptors within the C. elegans nervous system are partially overlapping (Tsalik et al., 2003; Chase et al., 2004; Sanyal et al., 2004; Suo et al., 2003), raising the possibility that different subnetworks within the nervous system function to temporally regulate behavioral buffering across development.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Tsalik et al., 2003; Chase et al., 2004; Sanyal et al., 2004; Suo et al., 2003.

claim: Different subnetworks within the nervous system may function to temporally regulate behavioral buffering across development.
source: Interestingly, the expression patterns of the three dopamine receptors within the C. elegans nervous system are partially overlapping (Tsalik et al., 2003; Chase et al., 2004; Sanyal et al., 2004; Suo et al., 2003), raising the possibility that different subnetworks within the nervous system function to temporally regulate behavioral buffering across development.
evidence: This is speculated based on the overlapping expression patterns of dopamine receptors.

claim: The function of serotonin receptors in maintaining patterns of roaming activity in unstressed individuals was shown to be modular across developmental stages.
source: Similarly, the function of serotonin receptors in maintaining patterns of roaming activity in unstressed individuals was also shown to be modular across developmental stages (Stern et al., 2017), suggesting a common principle of temporal regulation of behavior by neuromodulatory receptors.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Stern et al., 2017.

claim: There is a common principle of temporal regulation of behavior by neuromodulatory receptors.
source: Similarly, the function of serotonin receptors in maintaining patterns of roaming activity in unstressed individuals was also shown to be modular across developmental stages (Stern et al., 2017), suggesting a common principle of temporal regulation of behavior by neuromodulatory receptors.
evidence: This is inferred from the modular function of both dopamine and serotonin receptors.

claim: Under normal growth conditions, serotonin is known to regulate roaming behavior in C. elegans across all developmental stages.
source: Under normal growth conditions, serotonin is known to regulate roaming behavior in C. elegans across all developmental stages, (Flavell et al., 2013; Stern et al., 2017) and is required for long- and short-term associative olfactory memory (Jin et al., 2016; Zhang et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Flavell et al., 2013; Stern et al., 2017.

claim: Serotonin is required for long- and short-term associative olfactory memory.
source: Under normal growth conditions, serotonin is known to regulate roaming behavior in C. elegans across all developmental stages, (Flavell et al., 2013; Stern et al., 2017) and is required for long- and short-term associative olfactory memory (Jin et al., 2016; Zhang et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Jin et al., 2016; Zhang et al., 2005.

claim: In rodents, serotonin and dopamine interact to establish motor patterns.
source: In rodents, serotonin and dopamine interact to establish motor patterns (Sasaki-Adams and Kelley, 2001).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Sasaki-Adams and Kelley, 2001.

claim: The complexity of long-term behavioral responses to early stress may reflect a time integration of the function of multiple neuromodulators, each of them acting at different development times and with different intensity.
source: It is plausible that the complexity of long-term behavioral responses to early stress reflects a time integration of the function of multiple neuromodulators, each of them acting at different development times and with different intensity.
evidence: This is speculated based on the observed temporal segregation of dopamine and serotonin functions.

claim: Upon stress or another unpredictable environment, it will be beneficial for the population to dynamically reshape the variation across a spectrum of individuality dimensions so as to modify individual strategies and increase the population's chance of survival.
source: A plausible explanation for the coexistence of multiple individuality dimensions is that, upon stress or another unpredictable environment, it will be beneficial for the population to dynamically reshape the variation across a spectrum of individuality dimensions so as to modify individual strategies and increase the population's chance of survival (Cooper and Kaplan, 1982; Honegger and de Bivort, 2018).
evidence: This is speculated as a potential explanation and supported by citations to Cooper and Kaplan, 1982; Honegger and de Bivort, 2018.

claim: Neuromodulation was previously shown to affect levels of consistent individual biases.
source: Neuromodulation was previously shown to affect levels of consistent individual biases (Honegger et al., 2020; Kain et al., 2012; Pantoja et al., 2016; Stern et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Honegger et al., 2020; Kain et al., 2012; Pantoja et al., 2016; Stern et al., 2017.

claim: Underlying differences among individuals may include diversity in gene-expression patterns.
source: Underlying differences among individuals may include diversity in gene-expression patterns (Casanueva et al., 2012), nervous system structure (Witvliet et al., 2021; Brittin et al., 2021; Linneweber et al., 2020; Churgin et al., 2021), and underlying persistent differences in neuromodulatory parameters that have phenotypic effects under specific conditions (Marder et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Casanueva et al., 2012.

claim: Underlying differences among individuals may include diversity in nervous system structure.
source: Underlying differences among individuals may include diversity in gene-expression patterns (Casanueva et al., 2012), nervous system structure (Witvliet et al., 2021; Brittin et al., 2021; Linneweber et al., 2020; Churgin et al., 2021), and underlying persistent differences in neuromodulatory parameters that have phenotypic effects under specific conditions (Marder et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Witvliet et al., 2021; Brittin et al., 2021; Linneweber et al., 2020; Churgin et al., 2021.

claim: Underlying differences among individuals may include underlying persistent differences in neuromodulatory parameters that have phenotypic effects under specific conditions.
source: Underlying differences among individuals may include diversity in gene-expression patterns (Casanueva et al., 2012), nervous system structure (Witvliet et al., 2021; Brittin et al., 2021; Linneweber et al., 2020; Churgin et al., 2021), and underlying persistent differences in neuromodulatory parameters that have phenotypic effects under specific conditions (Marder et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Marder et al., 2022.

claim: Some of the variation, which is partially stochastic by nature, may generate different behavioral biases of individuals within isogenic populations.
source: It is plausible that some of this variation, which is partially stochastic by nature, may generate different behavioral biases of individuals within isogenic populations.
evidence: This is speculated as a potential explanation for inter-individual variation.

claim: Part of the temporal- or inter-individual variation in behavior may not directly rely on differences in neuromodulatory states over time or across individuals, but rather on the modification of behavioral sensitivity to underlying variations by specific neuromodulatory and environmental perturbations.
source: More generally, taking into consideration the complex relationship between different effects within a non-linear system (Félix and Barkoulas, 2015), part of the temporal- or inter-individual variation in behavior may not directly rely on differences in neuromodulatory states over time or across individuals, but rather on the modification of behavioral sensitivity to underlying variations by specific neuromodulatory and environmental perturbations (Maloney, 2021).
evidence: This is speculated based on the complexity of non-linear systems and supported by citations to Félix and Barkoulas, 2015; Maloney, 2021.
